title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

description: Join the LGBTQ+ Culture Center for World AIDS Day, an evening of remembrance, reflection, and hope featuring keynote speaker Ace Robinson, M.P.H., M.H.L., Director of Sexual & Gender Minority (Queer) Wellness at Duke University.       A nationally recognized HIV policy advocate and population health expert, Ace Robinson has spent more than two decades advancing health equity and supporting communities disproportionately impacted by HIV. title: World AIDS Day - Keynote: Ace Robinson, M.P.H., M.H.L.
description:
Join the LGBTQ+ Culture Center for World AIDS Day, an evening of remembrance, reflection, and hope featuring keynote speaker Ace Robinson, M.P.H., M.H.L., Director of Sexual & Gender Minority (Queer) Wellness at Duke University. 
A nationally recognized HIV policy advocate and population health expert, Ace Robinson has spent more than two decades advancing health equity and supporting communities disproportionately impacted by HIV. Throughout his career, he has held leadership roles with organizations including the National Minority AIDS Council (NMAC), Gay Men’s Health Crisis (GMHC), the Desmond Tutu Health Foundation in South Africa, and the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. 
In his keynote, “Willing Our Way to End the HIV Epidemic,” Robinson will explore the progress made in HIV prevention and treatment, the challenges that remain, and the collective action needed to build a future free from stigma, discrimination, and health inequities. 
Following the keynote, participants will have an opportunity to gather in community as we honor those lost to HIV/AIDS, recognize the resilience of people living with HIV, and recommit ourselves to creating a more just and compassionate future.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Baroque Orchestra – Ingrid Matthews, director
description: Repertoire to be announcedAbout the DirectorIngrid Matthews teaches baroque violin in the Historical Performance Institute at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. She served previously as music director of the Seattle Baroque Orchestra and has appeared as a soloist, guest director, and concertmaster for leading early music ensembles including the New York Collegium, Australian Brandenburg Orchestra, Boston Early Music Festival Orchestra, Ars Lyrica, Tafelmusik Baroque Orchestra, Musica Angelica, The Bach Sinfonia, Indianapolis Baroque Orchestra, and many others. She is also a member of San Francisco-based chamber ensemble Musica Pacifica and has held teaching residencies at the University of Southern California, University of Toronto, Oberlin College, Cornish College of the Arts, New England Conservatory, and others. First prizewinner in the 1989 Erwin Bodky International Competition for Early Music, Matthews herself has served as a juror for competitions such as the Maurice and Lillian Barbash International Bach Competition and the Indianapolis Early Music Competition. She has received high critical acclaim for her extensive discography; her recording of the Sonatas and Partitas for Unaccompanied Violin of J. S. Bach was named "top recommendation for this music...on either period or modern instruments" by American Record Guide, and her recording of Biagio Marini is included in the Norton Anthology of Music used by conservatories and universities worldwide.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: HIV/STI Testing
description: Free HIV Testing & Safer Sex Supplies at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center  Taking care of your sexual health is an important part of your overall well-being, and we're committed to making resources accessible, welcoming, and judgment-free.Positive Link (https://iuhealth.org/find-medical-services/positive-link-hiv-services) provides free and confidential HIV testing in Room 204 of the LGBTQ+ Culture Center every Thursday from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. during the academic year. During the summer, testing is available on the first and third Thursdays of each month.  In addition, during the academic year, the Monroe County Health Department offers free chlamydia and gonorrhea testing on the third Thursday of every month, also from 10:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. in Room 101.  The LGBTQ+ Culture Center also offers a variety of free safer sex supplies, including condoms, internal condoms, dental dams, lubricants, and educational materials on proper use. These resources are available to all students, free of charge. You can find them in the kitchenette area near the back entrance of the Center and are welcome to take what you need.  STI Testing & Safer Sex Resources Beyond Campus  Prioritizing your sexual health should be simple and accessible. In addition to services available at the LGBTQ+ Culture Center, students can receive testing on campus through the IU Student Health Center (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/medical/sti-testing/index.html) or visit several local organizations (https://healthcenter.indiana.edu/health-answers/sexual-health/sti-testing-resources.html) that offer free or low-cost testing and prevention services.  Many of these providers offer confidential care, safer sex supplies, and supportive information about prevention, treatment, and sexual wellness. If you're unsure where to start, we're happy to help connect you with resources that fit your needs.All Indiana University events, groups, activities, educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all members of the Indiana University community.

title: Scholarly Write-In
description:
Write and work in solidarity with other IU scholars. We offer a silent work environment with coffee and natural light. The write-in is open to all graduate students (at any stage of their degree program).

We will check in at the beginning of our meeting, set some goals together, then work independently for a few hours. Fifteen minutes prior to the close of the meeting, we will reconvene to update each other on our progress and set broad goals for the coming week.

This is a casual meeting – feel free to come for as much or as little time as you like, and only during the weeks that work for you. You are welcome and encouraged to work on anything that you need time and space for: participants regularly work on dissertations, course papers, syllabi and lesson plans, articles and pieces for publication, and grading. Our goal is to create a space where we can work together in solidarity on whatever projects we need to each week.

Meets weekly throughout the semester, Thursdays from 1-4pm. No meeting during Thanksgiving break.

Co-sponsored by Writing Tutorial Services and the IU Libraries.

title: 21JPSI Speaker Series "The Future of Space Security in Asia" (Prof. Saadia Pekkanen (University of Washington))
description: A public talk/Q&A about space security in Asia by one of the world's leading experts. Hodge Hall (HH) 2079 (corner of E 10th St and N Fee Lane)  This public event is open to all students, faculty, staff, and members of the community.Co-sponsored by the IU Institute for Korean Studies and Space Governance Lab. Please join us!Space has emerged as a consequential arena of strategic competition, defense, and conflict. Asia, with the greatest concentration of the world's top independent space powers, is at the forefront of these dynamics. Japan's growing capabilities, changing operational postures, and deepening space collaboration with the United States are contributing to – and helping shape – this evolving strategic environment, and broader prospects for war and peace.This event is co-sponsored by IU's Cybersecurity and Global Policy Program, the Department of Political Science, and the Space Governance Lab.  ————————————Saadia M. Pekkanen is the Job and Gertrud Tamaki Endowed Professor of International Studies, Adjunct Professor of Political Science, and Adjunct Professor of Law at the University of Washington in Seattle. She is founding director of the Program on Strategy, Policy, and Diplomacy Research (SPDR) at The Henry M. Jackson School of International Studies and the Founding Director of the Space Law, Data, and Policy Program (SPACE LDP) at the School of Law. Her research interests are in outer space security, diplomacy, and international affairs, with a focus on Japan and Asia. She has published widely, and is most recently co-editor of the special issue on Space Diplomacy: The Final Frontier of Theory and Practice, and co-editor of The Oxford Handbook of Space Security. She earned Master's degrees from Columbia University and Yale Law School, and a doctorate from Harvard University in political science. She is an elected member of the International Institute of Space Law (IISL) and a lifetime member of the Council of Foreign Relations (CFR). For further information please visit, saadiapekkanen.com.Adam LIFF (host/moderator) is Professor of East Asian International Relations at Indiana University's Hamilton Lugar School of Global and International Studies, where he also serves as Founding Director of its 21st Century Japan Politics and Society Initiative ("21JPSI"). He holds a Ph.D. and M.A. in Politics from Princeton University, a postgraduate research certificate in International Politics from the University of Tokyo, and a B.A. in East Asian Studies and Psychology from Stanford University All 21JPSI events are 100% in-person unless otherwise noted. title: Sarah Jarosz: 10 Years of Undercurrent
location: Buskirk-Chumley Theater,114 East Kirkwood Avenue, Bloomington, IN 47408, USA
description:
Originally from Wimberley, Texas, Sarah Jarosz is a six-time GRAMMY Award winning singer, songwriter and multi-instrumentalist. Since her recorded debut in 2009, she has released seven solo albums and two albums with I’m With Her, her band with Sara Watkins and Aoife O’Donovan.

In addition to her multiple GRAMMY, Americana Music Association, and Folk Alliance awards, her work has received widespread critical praise from publications including Rolling Stone, The New York Times, and USA Today. Jarosz has appeared three times on PBS’s legendary Austin City Limits television show and numerous times on A Prairie Home Companion, Live From Here, and the Grand Ole Opry. She is currently based in Nashville, Tennessee.

Jordan Tice is an award-winning guitarist and songwriter described by the Fretboard Journal as “quite simply, one of our favorite acoustic guitarists performing today.” He has 7 projects to his name as a solo artist and 6 as a founding member of the string band, Hawktail.

Equally virtuosic as a flatpicker and fingerstylist, and with a casual vocal style, Tice conjures ingredients from far-flung worlds with ease. His performances call upon the repertories of American and British Isles folk, bluegrass, blues and pop-oriented songs, and though his earlier releases are instrumental in focus, he has been carefully honing his craft as a singer-songwriter in his most recent work. This includes his albums Motivational Speakeasy (produced by Kenneth Pattengale of The Milk Carton Kids and praised by NPR Music as “a really wonderful record”), Wild Rose of Morning (a collaboration with Andrew Marlin and Christian Sedelmyer), and Badlettsville.

He has performed at festivals such as the Grey Fox Bluegrass Festival, Green Mountain Bluegrass and Roots, Red Wing Roots, Wintergrass Music Festival, and the Strawberry Music Festival and opened for artists like Watchhouse, I’m With Her, The Milk Carton Kids, and Madison Cunningham. In addition to his solo and collaborative work, he has performed and recorded as a sideman with Americana artists such as David Rawlings, Yola, Andrew Marlin and Aoife O’Donovan.

title: New Music Ensemble – David Dzubay, director; Dai Fujikura, guest composer; Sara Erb, alumna guest bassoon
description: Repertoire  Augusta Read Thomas: Solstice Ritual (2024)Donald Erb: The Towers of Silence (1974)Dai Fujikura: Bassoon Concerto No. 2 (2026)About the DirectorDavid Dzubay's compositions have been performed in the United States, Europe, Canada, Mexico, and Asia by the symphony orchestras of Aspen, Atlanta, Baltimore, Boston, Cincinnati, Detroit, Fort Wayne, Guangxi, Guiyang, Honolulu, Kansas City, Louisville, Memphis, Minnesota, Oregon, Oakland, St. Louis and Vancouver; the American Composers Orchestra, National Symphonies of Ireland and Mexico, New World Symphony, National Repertory Orchestra, and New York Youth Symphony; and ensembles including the Grossman Ensemble, Le Nouvel Ensemble Moderne, Onix, Manhattan and St. Louis Brass Quintets, Voices of Change, the Alexander, Orion and Pacifica string quartets, the League/ISCM, Earplay, and the San Francisco Contemporary Music Players. His music has been championed by conductors including James DePreist, George Hanson, Keith Lockhart, David Loebel, Michael Morgan, Eiji Oue, Richard Pittman, Iván del Prado, Mark Russell Smith, Lawrence Leighton Smith, Michael Stern, Carl Topilow, David Wiley, Kirk Trevor, Thomas Wilkins, and David Zinman. Honors include two Fromm Music Foundation commissions; Guggenheim, MacDowell, Yaddo, Copland House, and Djerassi fellowships; the Kuhmo Chamber Music Festival Composition Competition, Indianapolis Chamber Orchestra Composition Competition, Utah Arts Festival Commission, William Revelli and Walter Beeler Memorial Prizes, Wayne Peterson Prize; and grants from the Aaron Copland Fund for Music for two portrait CDs. Currently professor of music and director of the New Music Ensemble at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music in Bloomington, Dzubay was previously on the faculty of the University of North Texas in Denton. Since 2011, he has taught composition for three weeks each summer at the Brevard Music Center. From 1995 to 1998, he served as composer-consultant to the Minnesota Orchestra and during the 2005-06 season, he was Meet the Composer/American Symphony Orchestra League Music Alive Composer-in-Residence with the Green Bay Symphony Orchestra. Dzubay has conducted at the Tanglewood, Aspen, and June in Buffalo festivals as well as the National Symphony of Columbia, Grossman Ensemble, League of Composers Orchestra, Pittsburgh New Music Ensemble, Music from China, and Voices of Change.Five Friends Master Class Series – Honoring Robert SamelsThe Five Friends Master Class Series honoring the lives of five talented Jacobs School of Music students—Chris Carducci, Garth Eppley, Georgina Joshi, Zachary Novak, and Robert Samels—was established in 2012 with a gift of $1 million from the Georgina Joshi Foundation, Inc. This annual series of lectures, master classes, and residencies by a number of the world's leading musicians and teachers focuses on areas of interest most relevant to the lives of the five friends—voice performance, choral conducting, early music, music theory, composition, and opera. The Georgina Joshi Foundation was established in 2007 as the vision of Georgina Joshi's mother, Louise Addicott-Joshi, to provide educational and career development opportunities for young musicians and to encourage and support public performance of music. The gift to the school establishes a permanent way for the world to learn about each of the five friends, their musical talents and passions, and to encourage the development of similar talents and passions in current and future music students. The establishment of this endowment by the families is administered by the IU Foundation.  Bass-baritone and composer Robert Samels was born on June 2, 1981, and died in a plane crash on April 20, 2006. He was a doctoral student in choral conducting at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music and had studied voice with Giorgio Tozzi and Costanza Cuccaro. He began his vocal studies with Alfred Anderson at the University of Akron and Andreas Poulimenos at Bowling Green State University. Samels had recently appeared as Mr. Gibbs in the world premiere of Our Town by Ned Rorem, as Marco in the collegiate premiere of William Bolcom's A View from the Bridge, and as Joseph and Herod in the collegiate premiere of El Nino by John Adams. In September 2005, he conducted the premiere of his own opera, Pilatvs. As a member of the Wolf Trap Opera Company for 2006, he would have added three roles that summer, including Bartolo in Le Nozze di Figaro, Friar Laurence in Roméo et Juliette, and Pluto in Telemann's Orpheus. Other opera credits included the title roles of Don Pasquale and Il Turco in Italia, as well as Leporello in Don Giovanni, Falstaff in TheMerry Wives of Windsor, and Bottom in A Midsummer Night's Dream. In the summer of 2004, he performed Creon in the New York premiere of John Eaton's Antigone. Samels also frequently performed in the oratorio repertoire. In the spring of 2005, he was selected as a semi-finalist in the annual competition of the Oratorio Society of New York. He was an announcer with public radio station WFIU, as well as the host and producer of its Cantabile program. A soloist with Aguavá New Music Studio, he had recently performed a concert at the Library of Congress. Samels was an associate instructor in the Jacobs School's Music Theory Department, where was loved and admired by his students.

title: Daniel Luis Martinez: The Blueprint | Exhibition
location: The Contemporary Art Museum of Indianapolis
description: Opening reception: Friday, October 2, 2026, 6–10pm  Exhibition on view: October 2–December 18, 2026  For this exhibition, the blueprint is used as both a representational and conceptual departure point. Daniel Luis Martinez uses cyanotype printmaking and mixed-media drawing techniques as a generative process to imagine a speculative home on the CAMi campus. The hybrid drawings and prints featured in the exhibition explore the tactile middle-ground of the blueprint as a creative endeavor.  The series employs orthographic conventions typical of architectural drawing sets, though not as precise instructions for building. Rather, a layered and loose approach expresses ideas of home as an architectonic language.  Daniel Luis Martinez is a registered architect, educator, and co-founder of the multi-disciplinary design studio LAA Office, which explores the intersection of landscape, art, and architecture. His research and creative work investigate the potential of public art to generate alternative forms of placemaking. Martinez is Associate Professor and Director of the IU Eskenazi School's J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program (https://architecture.indiana.edu/index.html) in Columbus, Indiana.  Learn more about the exhibition at the CAMI website (https://camindy.org/exhibitions-all/theblueprint).
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Frances Lightbound: The Land Dissolves in Water | Exhibition
description: Lecture: October 27, 6:30–8pmExhibition: October 27–December 6, 2026, Mon.–Thur. 10am–4pm when IU classes are in session  Lightbound studies the production of space in urban environments, weaving narratives across photography, print, spatial interventions, and sculpture, with a focus on materials and sites in transition.  Architecture becomes an entry-point to questions of land use, ownership and access, bodily experience and perception, and timeframes ranging from the human to the geological. Lightbound invites viewers to consider and participate in the continual (re)construction of meaning in urban environments.  Frances Lightbound holds a B.A. from Glasgow School of Art, Scotland, and an M.F.A. from the School of the Art Institute of Chicago. Recent solo exhibitions include Louise Hopkins Center for the Arts (Lubbock, TX), RULE Gallery (Marfa, TX), and the John David Mooney Foundation (Chicago, IL); her work has been exhibited internationally at venues in London, Glasgow and Berlin. Lightbound is a Lecturer at School of the Art Institute of Chicago in the departments of Print media and Photography.The J. Irwin Miller Architecture Program Lecture and Exhibition Series brings prominent working artists and architects to Columbus. Lectures take place in the auditorium and exhibitions in the gallery, both located within The Republic Building, 333 Second Street in Columbus. The gallery is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. All events are free and open to the public.

title: In Search of Freedom: Stories of Afghanistan Exhibition
description: In Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistan  OPEN SEPTEMBER 4, 2026 - DECEMBER 4, 2026, MONDAY - FRIDAY 12-4 PM  OPEN 5-8 PM ON FIRST FRIDAYS OF THE MONTHIn Search of Freedom: Stories from Afghanistancelebrates the beauty, resilience, and rich cultural heritage of Afghanistan through an exhibition of oil paintings by Afghan artist Qahar Behzad, alongside the collaborative mural,August 15: A Mural for Afghanistan.Organized in partnership with Indiana University's Center for Refugee Studies and Exodus Refugee Immigration, the exhibition explores the humanity of the refugee experience through the lens of Afghanistan, inviting visitors to look beyond conflict and discover the stories and experiences of displaced people.The exhibition brings together Qahar's vibrant paintings - which honor Afghanistan's history, traditions, and everyday beauty - withAugust 15: A Mural for Afghanistan,a collaborative project led by Tiffany Black Behzad in collaboration with 59 Afghan evacuees at Camp Atterbury following the fall of Afghanistan to the Taliban on August 15, 2021. Developed through art therapy workshops with Afghan artists Zainab Ahmadi and Fawzia Abdaly, the mural preserves the participants' voices, memories, hopes, and resilience. The mural stands as a record of collective experience and a tribute to those who continue to seek safety, dignity, and freedom against all odds.Together, the artworks present a deeply human portrait of displacement, resilience, and belonging, inviting visitors to reflect on the the universal connections that unite us across borders, traditions, and generations, and the enduring human desire for freedom.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers
description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence)  Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. Documents signed by the two other signers—Philip Livingston of New York and James Smith of Pennsylvania—are on display in the North Gallery in The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment.

title: Byrnes Institute Colloquium Book Talk: "The Bolsheviks Survive: Petrograd 1919" with Janet Rabinowitch and Tatiana Saburova
description: Petrograd, the imperial capital and the urban stage upon which virtually the entire Russian Revolution was enacted, in 1919 struggled through a year of civil war, hunger, social upheaval, and political and economic challenges. Based on exhaustive research in previously closed Russian archives, Alexander Rabinowitch authoritatively presents an in depth look at how Petrograd's local Soviet government and Bolshevik Party organizations struggled to implement the Bolshevik Party program, fight domestic and foreign counterrevolutionaries, quiet labor unrest, and provide food, fuel, and education to the local population. The methods and strategies used by the government and party organizations to organize public life and fight enemies, domestic and foreign, not only preserved the infant Soviet regime but proved to be the first manifestation of what would become the one-party authoritarian Soviet political system.

title: Rethinking Refugee Integration: Evidence from Newly Resettled Afghans in the United States
description: U.S. refugee policy continues to emphasize rapid employment and economic self-sufficiency as primary indicators of successful integration. Drawing on a program of research with newly resettled Afghan households in Missouri and Oregon, this presentation examines refugee integration through a multidimensional lens that extends beyond employment and income.  Using survey data from Afghan households in St. Louis, Missouri (N = 184) and Portland, Oregon (N = 150), alongside a national sample of refugee households from the Annual Survey of Refugees (N = 1,386), we examine multidimensional deprivation and its determinants among refugees resettled in the United States. Findings reveal widespread multidimensional deprivation, affecting 62% of households in St. Louis, 74% in Portland, and 70% of the national refugee sample. Household size and English language proficiency emerged as consistent predictors of deprivation across settings. At the same time, local contexts mattered: lower housing costs and greater economic security in St. Louis were associated with lower rates of multidimensional deprivation compared with Portland.  To better understand how refugees experience integration beyond material conditions, we draw on a follow-up mixed-methods study of 203 Afghan households and five focus group discussions. Quantitative findings indicate that stronger social connectedness within Afghan communities was associated with higher quality of life, whereas integration with Americans was not. Qualitative findings revealed strong intra-ethnic social ties alongside limited bridging connections to the broader host society. Participants described declining quality of life during the first five years of resettlement despite a strong sense of community belonging.  Together, these findings challenge employment-centered approaches to refugee integration and highlight the importance of multidimensional frameworks that account for material well-being, social connectedness, and quality of life. description: Introducing Denny Love, a Los Angeles–based actor and comedian whose career seamlessly bridges prestige television, live comedy, and viral digital culture.
